claims.claim: A galaxy is a vast system of stars, planets, and clouds of gas and dust, all bound together by gravity.

Galaxies range enormously in size: the largest contain trillions of stars and can span more than a million light-years, while the smallest contain a few thousand stars and span a few hundred light-years.
Astronomer Edwin Hubble developed a system of classifying galaxies by their shape, sorting them into spiral, elliptical, and irregular categories, and his scheme is still in use.

Spiral galaxies have a central bulge, a flattened disk, and spiral arms; they contain a mix of young and old stars, with new star formation visible in the arms; about two-thirds of nearby spiral galaxies are barred spirals, whose arms begin at the ends of a central bar of stars.
Elliptical galaxies are smooth spheres or squashed ellipsoids made almost entirely of old stars, with no spiral arms and little gas and dust for new star formation.

Irregular galaxies lack the regular shapes of spirals and ellipticals, tend to be smaller and less luminous, and many are undergoing intense star formation; the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are well-known examples at a distance of a little more than 160,000 light-years.

Galaxies are organized into groups (roughly 100 or fewer members), clusters (which may contain thousands of galaxies), and superclusters (arrangements of groups and clusters that are not gravitationally bound); the Milky Way sits in the Local Group of more than 50 galaxies, which lies just off the edge of the Virgo cluster, within the Laniakea supercluster.

Redshift is the shift of a galaxy's spectral lines toward longer wavelengths, seen when the galaxy is moving away from us; the size of the shift indicates its velocity, and combined with distance measurements redshift is used to estimate the distances of faraway galaxies.

Most large galaxies have supermassive black holes at their centers; in active galaxies, matter spiraling toward the black hole forms a hot accretion disk that powers the brilliantly bright center astronomers call an active galactic nucleus.

The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy whose disk spans more than 100,000 light-years, with Earth located about halfway from the center, and the Sun takes about 240 million years to orbit the galactic center (reference only; the Milky Way is a sibling topic).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How universal are central supermassive black holes in galaxies?
positions: NASA: 'Most large galaxies have supermassive black holes at their centers.'

OpenStax 27.2: observations show all galaxies with a spherical concentration of stars — ellipticals and spirals with nuclear bulges — harbor giant black holes, with masses from just under 1 million up to at least 30 billion solar masses (with uncertainties above that).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson uses NASA's measured 'most large galaxies' phrasing and describes active galactic nuclei as the bright-center phenomenon of active galaxies, which is consistent with both sources; no claim made that every galaxy hosts one.

positions: Common informal usage sometimes treats superclusters as the largest bound structures.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson follows NASA explicitly: groups and clusters are gravitationally bound; superclusters are arrangements of them that are not bound; the common-mistake section flags this.

Supports: galaxy definition (stars, planets, gas, dust bound by gravity); size range (trillions of stars / more than a million light-years down to a few thousand stars / a few hundred light-years); galaxy ages 10-13.6 billion years; shapes (mostly spirals and ellipticals, plus irregulars); most large galaxies hosting supermassive black holes; groups (~100 or fewer members), clusters (thousands), superclusters (not gravitationally bound); Local Group (more than 50 galaxies, including Andromeda as nearest large neighbor), Virgo cluster, Laniakea supercluster; Milky Way reference only (spiral, disk more than 100,000 light-years, Earth about halfway from the center, ~240-million-year solar orbit).

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: Hubble's classification of galaxies by shape; spiral structure (central bulge, halo, disk, arms; mixture of young and old stars; star formation in arms; arms bluer with young stars and emission nebulae); about two-thirds of nearby spiral galaxies are barred spirals, with arms beginning at the ends of the bar; ellipticals (spheres/ellipsoids of almost entirely old stars, no arms, little dust); irregulars (Hubble's catchall category, lower masses and luminosities, often intense star formation; Large and Small Magellanic Clouds as examples at a little more than 160,000 light-years).

sourceRecords.title: Astronomy 2e, 27.2 Supermassive Black Holes: What Quasars Really Are
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: active galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGNs); galaxies with spherical star concentrations (ellipticals and spirals with nuclear bulges) harbor giant central black holes; central black hole masses range from just under 1 million to at least 30 billion solar masses; energy comes from material in a hot accretion disk spiraling toward the black hole; supermassive black hole accretion is the documented mechanism for bright galaxy centers.
